A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Low-density steel Mechanical properties Edge dislocation Slip band DO ordered domains
A B S T R A C T

The microstructure and mechanical properties of Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C (x = 4, 6, 8, 10) low-density steels were studied using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and tensile machine. It is found that the microstructure evolves with the increasing of Al content from a single austenite phase steel for 4 %Al, to a ferrite-based duplex steel for 8 %Al, but nearly a fully ferrite phase steel with 10 %Al. As the Al content is increased from 4 wt % to 8 wt %, the yield strength and tensile strength are significantly increased from 239 MPa to 552 MPa–455 MPa and 740 MPa, respectively, while the uniform elongation is only slightly decreased from 38.5 % to 31.0 %. However, as the Al content is increased up to 10 %, the yield strength is gradually increased to 585 MPa, but the tensile elongation is sharply decreased down to about 4.6 %. Based on the thorough microstructure examination of the dislocation type and dislocation pattern and the microstructure evolution during tensile deformation, it is concluded that the excellent combination of the mechanical property of the 8Al steel is realized by the activation of the edge-typed dislocation and dynamic slip band refinement in the ferrite grain mitigated by the surrounded austenite grains, which enhanced the strain hardening rate significantly. This study not only reveals a new ductility-enhancing mechanism of ferrite + austenite duplex steel, but also provides a new route for designing BCC based low-density steel with high strength and high ductility.
1. Introduction

As one of the new generation materials, the lightweight steel has been paid much more attention over the past two decades due to its excellent combination of mechanical properties and low density [1–6]. The lightweight steels mainly include austenitic low-density steel with high carbon, high manganese, and high aluminum contents, the duplex low-density steel with relatively low contents of carbon, manganese, and aluminum, and the ferritic low-density steel with the lowest contents of carbon, manganese, and aluminum [2]. Al-alloyed low-density steels exhibit an attractive combination of yield strength, tensile strength, elongation and work-hardening capacity [2,7–9]. The excellent me chanical properties of high stacking fault energy (SFE) austenitic low-density steel are attributed to the planar glide of dislocations and the dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR) mechanism [10–13]. The planar glide of dislocations in high stacking fault energy austenite originates from the “slip plane softening” effect caused by dislocation
shearing of ordered domains [12].

In ferritic low-density steel, plastic instability exists and is induced by the introduction of B2 and DO ordered domains [14–16]. It was found that the dislocations gradually transitioned from single mixed dislocations to paired screw dislocations with the increase of Al content in Fe-Al ferritic low-density steel [14,16], which was associated with low-energy screw dislocations [14] and high Peierls-Nabarro stresses [16]. In traditional fully body-centered cubic (BCC) alloys, the gliding velocities of edge dislocations are typically much higher than those of screw dislocations due to the low Peierls-Nabarro stresses [17–19]. As a result, edge dislocation segments are readily annihilated during defor mation, and screw dislocations survive in the deformed microstructure [20,21]. However, edge dislocations are observed in multi-component BCC phases, such as titanium alloys [22] and high-entropy alloys [20, 21]. In these alloys, the significant increase of Peierls-Nabarro stress for edge dislocation glide, caused by substantial local atomic volume mismatch or ordered domains, may effectively impede dislocation motion and consequently promote extensive dislocation multiplication [20]. However, edge dislocations in ordered ferrite have not been re ported to date in ferritic matrix lightweight steels.

The research on duplex low-density steels primarily focused on austenite-based duplex low-density steels [23–25]. The introduction of B2 and $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered phases into high-aluminum ferrite can bring a significant enhancement in yield strength, but simultaneously lead to an increase in brittleness [15,23,24,26,27]. It was found that B2 and DO3 ordered domains appear in Fe-Al alloys during the cooling process when the Al content exceeds 6.2 % [28,29]. In the Fe21Mn10Al1C5Ni light weight steel, dislocations within the B2 particles exhibit planar glide characteristics, which may be attributed to the dislocation shearing of $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ nanoparticles [24]. Furthermore, planar slip of dislocations asso ciated with the shearing of ordered structures has also been observed in titanium alloys [30,31] and high-entropy alloys [32]. Therefore, the dislocation deformation characteristics of ferrite will be significantly influenced by the interactions between dislocations and ordered phases. However, the systematic work in this aspect has not yet been conducted to investigate the work hardening mechanisms of high-aluminum ferritic matrix-based lightweight steels.

To address this issue of both dislocation patterns and work hardening behaviors, Fe35MnxAl0.1C (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) low-density steels were designed. Among them, Fe35Mn4Al0.1C is an austenitic lightweight steel, Fe35Mn6Al0.1C is an austenite based duplex lightweight steel, and Fe35Mn8Al0.1C and Fe35Mn10Al0.1C are ferrite based duplex lightweight steels. Tensile deformations were carried out to reveal the microstructural effects on the work hardening behaviors and mechanical properties of the designed steels. And both scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM) were applied to reveal the microstructure evolution in terms of dislocation patterns of the designed steel during deformation process. The effects of micro structure on the dislocation type, dislocation pattern, work hardening behavior and mechanical property will be discussed, which is expected to give a thorough understanding on the evolution of dislocation pattern and the work hardening behavior of the ferrite-based duplex lightweight steel.
2. Materials and experimental details

Four ingots with nominal compositions of Fe-35Mn-xAl-1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) were prepared via vacuum induc tion melting under a high-purity Ar atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 1150 <sup>◦</sup>C for 4 h, and subsequently hot-forged into rods with a diameter of 16.5 mm. The bars were solution-treated at $1 0 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ $^ { \mathrm { f o r ~ 2 ~ h , } }$ followed by oil quenching, to achieve a microstructure with nearly equiaxed grains. For simplicity, the four solution-treated steels are hereafter referred to as 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels, respectively. The compositions of the solution-treated samples were examined by the wet-chemical analysis, and the results were shown in Table 1. The compositions of austenite phase and ferrite phase of the designed steels were investigated using the electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). The carbon content in austenite was calculated using the chemical compo sition lever rule [1,24]. The densities of the investigated steels, measured using the principle of Archimedes, are 7.42, 7.18, 6.99, and $6 . 8 4 ~ \mathrm { g ~ c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , respectively.

3. Results
3.1. Initial microstructures

The microstructures of the 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels after solu tion treatment are shown by the phase distribution maps in Fig. 1(a–d). EBSD analysis indicates that 4Al steel is a single-phase face-centered cubic $( { \mathrm { F C C } } ) \ Y$ austenite lightweight steel, 6Al steel is an austenite-based duplex lightweight steel, and 8Al and 10Al steels are ferrite-based duplex lightweight steels. It also shows that the microstructures with quasi-equiaxed grains are obtained under the solution treatment con ditions. It can be observed that the austenite grains contain numerous annealing twin boundaries (represented by white lines).

Fig. 1(e–h) shows the selected area diffraction patterns (SADPs) of 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels along the [100] zone axis of the austenite grains, where obvious satellite diffraction spots can be seen near the γ diffraction spots. The satellite diffraction spots near the $\gamma$ diffraction spots are related to the concentration fluctuations of Al and C atoms [11, 36], indicating that spinodal decomposition occurred during quenching. Very weak diffraction spots are identified at the {110} positions in 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels. In previous studies, this kind of ordered structure is revealed to be an $\mathrm { L } 1 _ { 2 }$ type short-range ordered crystal structure [11,37]. It can be seen that the intensity of these satellite diffraction spots de creases with increasing of the nominal Al content, which is revealed to be an $\mathbf { L } 1 _ { 2 }$ type short-range ordered crystal structure.

Fig. 1(i–k, m) shows the selected area diffraction patterns (SADPs) of 6Al, 8Al and 10Al steels along the $[ 1 1 0 ] _ { \alpha }$ zone axis of the ferrite grains, where distinct superlattice diffraction spots are observed. The maximum sizes of $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains in the 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels are estimated to be approxi mately 2.0 nm, 2.1 nm, and 19 nm, respectively. The size of the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains increases with the increase of the nominal aluminum content, suggesting that Al promotes the precipitation of $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains. In addition, acicular precipitates are observed within the ferrite grains of the 10Al steel, as shown in Fig. 1(o and p). It can be observed that Mn and C are significantly enriched in the acicular pre cipitates, while Al is depleted. The precipitates are identified as 18R martensite formed within the ferrite of the Fe-Mn-Al-C alloy during quenching [38–41]. This type of acicular martensite can significantly reduce the ductility of ferrite [42]. The TEM EDS mapping analysis in dicates that the 18R martensite is rich of manganese and carbon, as displayed in Fig. 1(p).

X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was conducted to further examine the phase composition and mass fractions in the lightweight steels, as presented in Fig. 2(a). The results indicate that the mass fractions of ferrite are 75.7 % and 98.1 % for 8Al and 10Al steels, respectively. The microhardness of austenite and ferrite in the designed steels is shown in Fig. 2(b). It can be seen that the microhardness of ferrite is significantly higher than that of austenite, indicating that ferrite acts as a strength ening phase in the designed steels.

text: Based on above analysis on the microstructure of the low-density steels with different Al content as shown in Fig. 1. it can be concluded that the microstructure of the low-density steel is strongly affected by the aluminum content, giving nearly full austenite microstructure for 4 %Al and 6 %Al,ferrite based duplex microstructure for 8 %Al, but nearly full ferrite microstructure for 10 % AL. Furthermore, in the austenite phase, the short-range ordering of Al and C could be found in the austenite phase of the low-density steel with aluminum evolved from 6 % to 10 %. In the ferrite phase, both B2 and $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ could be found in the ferrite phase, indicating that both ordered phases are easily developed in the ferrite phase.
3.2. Mechanical properties

The typical tensile engineering stress-strain curves and mechanical properties of 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels are shown in Table 3 and Fig. 3(a and b). It can be observed that as the Al content increases from 4 wt% to 8 wt%, the yield strength and tensile strength increase from 239 MPa to 552 MPa–455 MPa and 740 MPa, respectively. while the uniform elongation only decreases from 38 % to 31 %. However, as the Al con tent increased up to 10 %, the vield strength is increased to 585 MPa, but the tensile elongation is only about 4.6 %, exhibiting the brittle char acteristics. As demonstrated in Section 3.1, the degradation in plasticity of the 10Al steel can be attributed to the coarsening of $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains [15] and the formation of 18R martensite [42].

Fig. 3 (c, d) presents the true stress-strain curves and the corre sponding strain hardening curves for the 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al steels. It can be seen that the 4Al and 6Al steels exhibit typical three-stage strain hardening characteristics, labeled as A, D and E, whereas the 8Al steel displays five distinct strain hardening stages, labeled as A, B, C, D and $\mathrm { E } ,$ which is similar to the strain hardening behavior exhibited by high carbon, high-aluminum austenitic lightweight steels. This indicates that the deformation mechanism of the designed 8Al ferrite-based duplex lightweight steels differs from that of conventional ferritebased duplex steels [43,44]. Fig. 3 (e) presents the evolution of micro hardness with strain for the 4Al and 8Al steels it can be observed that the microhardness of austenite in both steels increases with increasing strain. However, the microhardness of ferrite in the 8Al steel initially decreases and then increases with strain. That is, the ferrite in the 8Al steel exhibits softening in the early stages of deformation, indicating differences in the deformation mechanisms between ferrite and austenite in the 8Al steel

text: 3.3. Deformed microstructure characteristics

The microstructure of the uniform deformation zone of the experi mental steels after tensile deformation is shown in Fig. 4. Due to the plastic instability of the 10Al steel, the microstructures after fracture at \~3 % engineering strain are shown in Fig. 4(g–i). It can be observed that the deformation mechanisms of austenite $( \mathrm { F i g } , 4 ( \mathbf { a } , \mathbf { b } , \mathbf { d } , \mathbf { e } , \mathbf { g } ) )$ and ferrite (Fig. 4(c–f, h, i)) are distinctly different. The microstructure of the austenite after tensile deformation is characterized by dislocation cell blocks regardless of the aluminum content, as shown in Fig. $4 ( \mathbf { a } , \mathbf { b } , { \mathrm { d } } ) _ { \mathbf { a } }$ which is common in low-carbon or low-aluminum lightweight steels [1, 45,46]. Additionally, a small number of deformation twins are observed in 8Al steel (Fig. 4(e)), which is associated with the localization of stress [1,47]. Fig. 4 (g) shows that the 10Al steel exhibits complex planar slip characteristics during the early deformation stage of austenite, which is similar to the deformation structure of the 6Al steel reported in our previous study [1]. The difference in dislocation deformation structure between this kind of low carbon austenitic lightweight steel and the traditional high carbon austenitic lightweight steel may be associated with the carbon induced suppression of cross-slip [46] and the devel: opment of the ordered structure [11].

It is very interesting that the dislocations in ferrite exhibit distinct planar slip characteristics, as shown in Fig. 4(c–f, h, i), which is quite rare in BCC structures [20.21]. It can be observed that the ferrite dislocation structure in 8Al steel exhibits a more pronounced planar slip characteristic compared with that in 6Al steel, indicating that the in crease in Al content may promote planar slip of ferrite dislocations. However, the increase in Al content also makes the 10Al steel particu larly brittle. Fig. 4(h, i) shows that only a small number of long straight dislocations are activated in the ferrite matrix. These long straight dis locations are identified as screw dislocations based on the discussion in Section 4.1. Brittle fracture caused by the activation of only a few long straight screw dislocations has also been observed in the TiZrHfNb0.4 BCC high-entropy alloy [20]. The planar slip of dislocations in ferrite will be discussed in detail in Section 4.2.
To further understand the deformation mechanism of this ferrite based lightweight steel, the microstructures of 8Al steel at different engineering strains are characterized, as shown in Fig. 5.

text: When the engineering strain reaches 3 %, planar dislocation slip along the slip planes and distinct cross-slip are observed in the austenite $\left( \mathrm { F i g . ~ 5 ~ ( a ) } \right)$ , while the ferrite is primarily characterized by a planar dislocation structure (Fig. 5 (b)). Fig. 5(c) presents a magnified view of the region marked in Fig. 5(b), where it can be observed that edge dis locations, mixed dislocations, and long straight screw dislocations are activated in ferrite of 8Al steel and form slip bands, which is different from the local screw dislocations in ferrite of 10Al steel. As the strain further increases to 10 %, cross-slip of dislocations in austenite becomes more pronounced (Fig. 5(d)). and the slip bands composed of dislocations in ferrite continue to evolve (Fig. 5(e)). When the engineering strain further increases to 20 %, the dislocation cell blocks (Fig. 5(f)) and dislocation cells (Fig. 5(g)) are formed in the austenite, and the slip bands in the ferrite are further refined (Fig. 5(h)). When the engineering strain reaches 28 %, the dislocation cell blocks (Fig. 5(i)) and dislocation cells (Fig. 5(j)) in the austenite are further refined, and a small number of deformation twins are formed due to the localization of stress (Fig. 5 (k)) [1]. Fig. 5(l) displays the dislocation structure in ferrite at 28 % engineering strain, revealing continued refinement of slip bands along with distinct cross-slip of dislocations. The orientation dependence of dislocation cell blocks and dislocation cell substructures in austenite has been analyzed in detail in the literature [1,45,46]. The average slip band (SB) spacing, dislocation cell block (DCB) size, and dislocation cell (DC) size in austenite, as well as the average slip band spacing in ferrite at different deformation stages, are statistically analyzed, as shown in Fig. 6.
4. Discussion
4.1. Identification of dislocation types in ferrite of 8Al and 10Al steel

There are significant differences in the micro-deformation behavior in ferrite of 10Al steel and 8Al steel, which are closely related to the activation of different types of dislocations. Here, the two-beam diffraction mode has been employed to investigate the types of dislo cations in ferrite of 10Al steel and 8Al steel. To better observe the dis locations, the samples are pre-deformed to the 3 % engineering strain. Fig. 7(a–f) presents the dislocation structures in ferrite of 10Al steel using the different g diffraction vectors near the [111] zone axis.

To identify the Burgers vector b of the ferrite, the g⋅b analyses are conducted. When g = [10 1] and $g = [ 1 \overline { { 1 } } 0 ]$ operating vector, some long straight dislocations systematically lose contrast (Fig. 7(a and b)), whereas when $g = [ 0 \mathrm { ~ \overline { { 1 } } ~ }$ 1] operating vector, all dislocations are visible (Fig. 7(c)). It can be concluded that the Burgers vector b is determined to be $a / 2 [ 1 1 1 ]$ by the $g \cdot b = 0$ analysis of the ferrite in 10Al steel, as shown in Fig. 7(a–c). Similarly, the Burgers vector of dislocations in ferrite of 8Al steel is also analyzed near the [111] zone axis, as shown in Fig. 7 $( { \pmb g } - { \bf l } ) .$ . Some dislocations systematically lost contrast under the [0 1 1] and [1 10] operating vector conditions. Subsequently, the Burgers vec tor b is also determined to be a/2[111] through the g⋅b = 0 analysis of the ferrite in 8Al steel.

Fig. 7(a–l) shows that the dislocation structures are quite different although the Burgers vectors of dislocations in ferrite of both 10Al steel and 8Al steel are of the $a / 2 < 1 1 1 > \mathrm { t y p e . A }$ predominant fraction of the dislocations in the ferrite of 10Al steel are identified as long straight screw dislocations, and their distribution is non-uniform, as shown in Fig. 7(a–f). These long straight screw dislocations are commonly observed in Fe-Al ordered alloys [14–16,48], which can be attributed at least partially to the significant energy difference between edge and screw dislocations, where the energy of screw dislocations is notably lower than that of edge dislocations [14].

Comparing with the long straight screw dislocations in 10Al steel, a substantial number of edge dislocations and mixed dislocations with near-edge character are uniformly distributed in the ferrite phase of 8Al steel. This homogeneous distribution of dislocations can effectively mitigate brittle fracture caused by stress concentration. It is reported in conventional body-centered cubic (BCC) alloys, the gliding velocities of edge dislocations are typically much higher than those of screw dislo cations [18,19], owing to the lower resistance stress. Consequently, the edge segments are more readily annihilated within BCC alloys, leaving screw dislocations as the predominant type in the deformed micro structures [21]. However, edge dislocations have also been reported in the BCC-structured Mo-Nb-Ti multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) [49] and Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb high-entropy alloy (HEA) [20]. The local chemical fluctuations in these alloys result in relatively high glide resistance for edge dislocations on the glide plane, making it less likely for edge dis: locations to annihilate. Similarly, B2 and DO ordered domains increase the resistance stress to the glide of edge dislocations in the ferrite of 8Al steel, which reduces the glide velocity of the edge dislocations and consequently leads to a significant multiplication of edge dislocations in 8Al steel.

text: Fig. 7(j–l) displays the dislocation structures at the ferrite-austenite phase interface. It can be observed that edge dislocations are more readily activated at the grain boundaries, which can be explained by the high stress present at these boundaries. It is reported that back stresses are generated in the soft phase, and forward stresses are developed in the hard phase during the deformation of heterogeneous structures [50]. In this case, the high stresses at ferrite grain boundaries, together with the stress-multiplication effect [51], facilitate the collective glide of dislo cations on the same slip plane. Additionally, approximately 24.3 % austenite in 8Al steel, acting as a soft phase, can effectively alleviate stress localization within the ferrite and enhance the deformation of the ferrite to higher stresses. It is particularly interesting that edge, mixed, and screw dislocations in ferrite all exhibit a typical planar slip char acteristic, which will be discussed in Section 4.2

The above analysis reveals that dislocations in the ferrite phase of 10Al steel are predominantly identified as long straight screw disloca tions, whose localized distribution contributes to brittle fracture behavior. In contrast, the ferrite of 8Al steel produces a significant number of edge dislocations and mixed dislocations with edge character, which markedly enhances the deformation capability of the 8Al steel ferrite.
4.2. The planar slip of dislocations in ferrite

In body-centered cubic (BCC) materials, screw dislocations typically exhibit pronounced cross-slip behavior due to their non-planar glide characteristics [52], which is fundamentally linked to the asymmetric core structure of screw dislocations and their high Peierls-Nabarro stress [53,54]. Interestingly, both edge and screw dislocations in 8Al steel and 10Al steel show distinct planar slip, as illustrated in Figs. 5 and 7. Studies demonstrate that the interaction between dislocations and or dered structures can lead to planar slip of dislocations, as observed in titanium alloys [30,31], FCC-structured Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys [12,13], and BCC-structured TiZrHfNbTa0.2 high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [32].

Fig. 8 shows the planar slip of dislocation in ferrite grains of 8Al steel and 10Al steel to reveal the deformation behaviors, which is controlled by the interaction between dislocation and the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered superlattice in the ferrite. It is worth noting that in the 10Al steel, dislocation pairing is extremely pronounced, with up to six dislocation pairs observed and dislocation spacings as small as approximately 3 nm, demonstrating pronounced paired super-dislocation characteristics. It can be observed that the large sized $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains in 10Al steel cannot be completely sheared (Fig. 8(c)), while the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains in 8Al steel can be completely sheared along the dislocation line direction and the slip plane direction (Fig. 8(f)). When the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains are destroyed by dislocations, anti-phase boundaries (APBs) are left behind [16]. The attractive force generated by APB energy leads to the pairing of dislocations. Studies on Fe-Al alloys demonstrate that APB energy in creases with Al content [14,55]. Consequently, the APB-induced attractive force in ferrite of 10Al steel becomes substantially stronger than that in ferrite of 8Al steel, resulting in more pronounced dislocation pairing in the 10Al alloy. Once the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domain is completely sheared, no anti-phase boundaries (APBs) will be generated by subse quent dislocations [13]. The size of the superlattice ordered domains can be estimated by multiplying the number of paired dislocations by the Burgers vector [12].

It can be observed that dislocations are composed of a multitude of dislocation dipoles, and the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ superlattice is sheared along dislocation line and slip plane by a large number of these dislocation dipoles. These findings are in agreement with observations reported in Refs. $[ 1 2 , 1 3 , 3 0 , 3 1 ]$ where sheared LRO clusters are proposed to cause planar slip.
4.3. Strain hardening behavior of 8Al steel

Fig. 3(d) reveals that 8Al steel exhibits multi-stage strain hardening, which is associated with the dynamic slip band refinement mechanism in ferrite. In stage A, the movement of dislocations leads to a sharp decrease in the strain hardening rate. In stage B, a reduction in the strain hardening rate is caused by the slip plane softening effect induced by dislocation shearing of the $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ long-range ordered domains [13]. In stage $\mathrm { C } ,$ the passing stress generated by slip bands of stored dislocations has been demonstrated to be the primary contributor to strain hardening [12]. With the increase of strain, the number of slip bands increases, the spacing between slip bands decreases, and the passing stress rises, which leads to an increase in the strain hardening rate. In stage D, with the continued increase of strain, the slip bands become nearly saturated, and cross-slip of dislocations is activated, which leads to a decrease in the strain hardening rate. In stage $\mathrm { E } ,$ localization of stress results in a rapid decline in the strain hardening rate and leads to plastic failure.

The deformation structures of ferrite and austenite in 8Al steel are dominated by dislocations until a small amount of deformation twins are activated in austenite near the maximum force. Therefore, the excellent strain hardening performance of 8Al steel is attributed to the refinement of ferrite slip bands and austenite dislocation cells. 5. Conclusion

The initial microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation microstructure evolution of Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C (x = 4, 6, 8, 10 wt%) lowcarbon lightweight steels were investigated. This study not only reveals a new ductility-enhancing mechanism of ferrite + austenite duplex steel, but also provides a new route for designing BCC based low-density steel with high strength and high ductility. text: 1. With increasing Al content, the phase constitution transitions sequentially from single-phase austenite (4Al steel) to austenitematrix duplex (6Al steel), then to ferrite-matrix duplex structures (8Al and 10Al steels). $\mathrm { D O } _ { 3 }$ ordered domains coexist within both the B2 ordered domains and the ferrite, exhibiting progressive size enlargement with higher Al concentrations.

2. The 8Al steel exhibits multi-stage strain hardening characteristics due to planar slip in ferrite. The dislocation structure in ferrite ex hibits distinct planar slip, forming slip bands whose spacing de creases during straining, in accordance with the dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR) mechanism.

3. The ferritic dislocation structure in 10Al steel is predominantly characterized by localized long straight screw dislocations, which leads to plastic instability in 10Al steel, whereas in 8Al steel, it is characterized by a uniform distribution of long straight screw and edge dislocations. The high stress at the austenite-ferrite interface facilitates the activation of edge dislocations in ferrite.

4. The size of the shear zone is estimated based on the number of paired dislocations at slip band fronts. The estimated size in 8Al steel is less than 1.5 nm, which is very close to the TEM-observed value of less than 2.1 nm. The estimated size in 10Al steel is less than 3.0 nm, which is much smaller than the TEM-observed value of less than 19.0 nm.

5. It is found that as the Al content increases from 4 % to 8 %, the yield strength and tensile strength increase from 239 (+7) MPa and 552 (±12) MPa to 455 (±10) MPa and 74 (±14) MPa, respectively, while the uniform elongation only decreases from 38.5 (±2.0) % to 31.0 (±1.3) %. The synergistic operation of edge dislocation activity and DSBR effect in ferritic matrices underlies the superior strengthductility balance observed in the 8Al ferrite-based duplex light weight steel.
